source: Goecks & Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT
finding: An LLM given doctrine excerpts in context writes a militarised StarCraft II course of action in seconds. Text-only COA-GPT, with no human feedback, beat both published RL baselines on mean total reward.
numbers: 5 COAs per variant x 10 simulations = 50 rollouts per baseline. Best variant (vision + two feedback rounds) scored 3.4% below an expert human (15 trials), who had the lowest casualties. The RL baseline needed 112 thousand battles / 70 million timesteps.
limits: LLM COAs were one-shot orders with no mid-battle control; friendly casualties stayed higher than every baseline. One scenario (TigerClaw), mostly deterministic game, one human expert, RL numbers copied from earlier papers. Not a test of the doctrine rule of several COAs.
agent_relevance: A generated plan can be scored by simulation. Generate plus test beats a trained policy here, but the test is a game engine, not an enemy mind.

source: Goecks & Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT, feedback loop
finding: Human feedback rounds raised mean reward and cut its spread. Feedback was a short sentence, for example 'make sure both aviation units engage the enemy aviation'.
numbers: Variants COA-GPT+H1 and +H2 (text) and COA-GPT-V+H1/H2 (vision). Standard deviation fell after each round; the human expert had the largest variance.
limits: Feedback came from the authors acting as commander. No count of how often feedback helped or hurt. Reward formula hand-made (+10 / -10 per bridge crossing or unit).
agent_relevance: Supports a commander-in-the-loop revise step after test (S4 back to S3). The gain is lower variance as well as a higher mean.

source: Goecks & Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT, vision ablation
finding: Adding one map image (COA-GPT-V) gave no gain over text-only before feedback. Only after feedback did the vision variant pull ahead.
numbers: Same 50-rollout design per variant. Text-only already beat the prior state of the art without the image.
limits: No significance test; only mean and std shown in figures.
agent_relevance: More input modality did not replace the test-and-revise loop.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine wargame
finding: Wargame with 214 national-security experts in 48 teams vs simulated LLM teams in a fictional US-China crisis. High-level agreement, but clear quantitative and qualitative differences in single actions.
numbers: Of 21 possible actions per game, simulated teams matched human frequency on 16 (GPT-3.5), 10 (GPT-4) and 9 (GPT-4o). Human treatment effects were reproduced by only some model settings (Table 1).
limits: Simulated players were sampled from profiles of the first 107 humans. One fictional scenario. Results depend on the LLM and on whether it decides for the team or simulates dialog.
agent_relevance: An LLM stand-in for a red or blue team does not match experts on single choices. Use it for breadth of options, not as the final judge.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine, dialog and traits
finding: Simulated team dialog was low quality and kept a farcical harmony. Prompting extreme traits ('pacifist', 'aggressive sociopath') made no significant difference.
numbers: No significant difference across player backgrounds for all actions and all LLMs. Probability of staying aggressive in move 2 after aggressive move 1 was 0.94 to 1.00 across LLM settings; after de-escalation 0.65 to 0.86.
limits: Conditional-probability values read from a garbled two-column table; check the PDF before quoting.
agent_relevance: One model told to play an adversary has little persona range. A red-team operator needs real differences in goals and doctrine.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine, instruction following
finding: When briefing priorities were removed, LLM choices shifted strongly. GPT-3.5 became likelier to 'fire at Chinese vessels'. Models differ in violence after the same strategic instruction.
numbers: GPT-3.5 raised 'fire' and full-automation AI-weapon choices; GPT-4 and GPT-4o mostly shifted toward cautious uses of the AI weapon.
limits: Effect sizes are in figures, not text. One scenario.
agent_relevance: Commander intent in the prompt steers an LLM plan strongly. Keep intent and constraints explicit and re-check them after each revision.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models
finding: Eight LLM nation agents in turn-based wargames: all five off-the-shelf models escalated, with sudden jumps and arms-race dynamics. Rare nuclear use.
numbers: 10 simulations per model per scenario, 14 simulated days, 3 scenarios, 5 models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 2, Llama-2-70B Chat, GPT-4-Base). No model showed significant de-escalation. GPT-3.5 escalation score rose from 10.15 to 26.02 (+256%) in the neutral scenario.
limits: Most start-vs-end differences were not statistically significant. Scoring weights are author-designed. A world-model LLM, not a rules engine, decided consequences.
agent_relevance: LLM adversaries drift toward escalation. Test each COA against several enemy replies, including de-escalating ones, and do not let one LLM play both sides.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks, model contrast
finding: Models differ a lot. Llama-2-Chat and GPT-3.5 were most violent apart from GPT-4-Base. GPT-4 took the fewest violent or nuclear actions; Claude 2.0 had the smallest tendency to escalate. Reasoning text cited deterrence and first-strike logic.
numbers: Table 2 gives shares of non-violent, violent and nuclear actions per model; only the ranking was read here.
limits: 2023 models only. Reported reasoning may not be the true cause of the action.
agent_relevance: Model choice is a moderator. Run a red-team role on more than one model and compare.

source: Hogan & Brennen (2024) Open-Ended Wargames with LLMs
finding: IQT Labs tool lets LLMs play every role and adjudicate in a free-text wargame, with or without humans. A design and demo paper with no outcome measure.
numbers: No sample sizes or scores. Example scenario: the tabletop exercise HAIWIRE with random incidents and injects.
limits: Qualitative only; authors note LLMs are weak at modelling player background.
agent_relevance: Shows a cheap harness for COA-versus-enemy-move play but gives no evidence it improves plans.

source: Matlin et al. (2026) Shall We Play a Game? Language Models for Open-ended Wargames
finding: Scoping review of 223 de-duplicated AI-in-wargame papers (to May 1, 2026). Only 20 (9%) let a language model both choose actions and adjudicate consequences.
numbers: 223 papers; 20 give the model both open-ended roles.
limits: Review of design choices, not outcomes. Counts depend on their rubric.
agent_relevance: Most studies test a player model against a fixed referee. Whether an LLM can judge consequences of a COA is the least tested link.

source: Yin et al. (2025) WGSR-Bench: situational awareness (MM-SA-Bench)
finding: On a wargame multimodal situational-awareness test, humans from military academies and gamer groups scored 79.9; the best AI model scored 58.2. The gap was largest in complex situation analysis.
numbers: Humans 79.9 vs best model 58.2 (21.7 gap); worst models 27.0 and 26.4. Complex Situation Analysis: humans 85.9% vs best multimodal model 37.5%. Simple spatial relations were closer (71.3% vs 80.1%; 69.2% vs 80.9%).
limits: Multiple-choice format; 2025 Chinese multimodal models, not frontier reasoning models. Human sample size not extracted.
agent_relevance: The weak step is reading the whole situation, before any COA is written. Put situation analysis before generation.

source: Yin et al. (2025) WGSR-Bench: opponent risk modelling
finding: Text tasks on opponent risk modelling: LLMs did well on long-term reward attribution but poorly on short-term attribution and on predicting an opponent's strategy under risk.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1: 84.0 long-term reward attribution (human 83.3) vs 45.2 short-term (human 87.8); about 31.1 on high-risk strategy prediction. One prediction score 42.2 vs human 88.5.
limits: Numbers are scattered through the text; which sub-task each belongs to needs checking in the paper. Part of the scoring uses an LLM judge.
agent_relevance: Predicting the enemy reply, the core of COA analysis, is where models lag humans most. Do not trust a model's own war-game of the enemy unchecked.

source: Huang et al. (2024) LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking a model to review and fix its answer does not help and often hurts. Earlier gains used the ground-truth label to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA: 75.8 baseline, 38.1 after round 1. GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7 after round 2. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49 to 43. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Question answering and math with known answers, not planning. The paper endorses external feedback.
agent_relevance: A model grading its own COA is weak evidence. The test step needs an outside check: a rule, a simulation, another model or a human.

source: Huang et al. (2024), multi-agent debate vs self-consistency
finding: Replicating multi-agent debate (3 agents, 2 rounds, full GSM8K test set) found it does not beat plain self-consistency at equal numbers of responses.
numbers: GSM8K, gpt-3.5-turbo-0301: standard 76.7; debate about 83.2; self-consistency with matching calls 82.5 to 88.2 (rows garbled in extracted text).
limits: Pairing of rows in Table 7 not certain. The original debate paper used 100 examples.
agent_relevance: Several voices arguing is not shown better than several independent samples plus a vote. Debate-style red teaming must beat a vote.

source: Liang et al. (2024) Multi-agent debate for divergent thinking
finding: Debate with a judge was proposed to fix 'Degeneration-of-Thought': a model that is sure of its first answer cannot produce new ideas when it reflects on itself.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive Arithmetic: GPT-3.5-Turbo 26.0; +CoT 28.0; +Self-Consistency 29.5; +Self-Reflect 27.5; +MAD 37.0; GPT-4 51.0. Translation: small gains.
limits: Small test sets; gains on hard counter-intuitive items, near zero on standard ones. Published before Huang et al.'s critique.
agent_relevance: Supports a forced-critic step on hard problems; self-reflection locked onto first answers, forced disagreement did not.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) Planning abilities of o1
finding: Reasoning model o1-preview jumps on classical planning but is fragile: 97.8% on Blocksworld, much lower when disguised or when plans are long.
numbers: Blocksworld 2-16 steps: 97.8%. Mystery Blocksworld 52.8%. Randomized Mystery 37.3% (earlier LLMs near 0%). Plans of 20-40 steps: 23.63% on 110 instances. Unsolvable instances flagged correctly 27% (Blocksworld) and 16% (randomized). Best non-reasoning model, LLaMA 3.1 405B: 62.6%.
limits: Toy domains with a formal verifier; Fast Downward gets 100% in less time and cost. Not military planning.
agent_relevance: Long plans and 'no feasible plan' cases are where generated plans fail. A many-step COA needs a verifier, and the agent must be able to say none works.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs can't plan, but can help planning (LLM-Modulo)
finding: Position paper: LLMs are idea generators; correctness must come from external critics and verifiers in a generate-test loop. Same shape as doctrine's develop-then-wargame cycle.
numbers: Cites that on average only about 12% of LLM-generated plans were executable and correct; LLM-Modulo reached 82% on a Blocksworld subset and 70% in Logistics.
limits: Mostly argument plus earlier results; the 82% and 70% come from other papers.
agent_relevance: Strong match to S3/S4: the model proposes several COAs, separate coded critics reject them.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024), claims of self-verification
finding: Authors say LLM self-verification claims hold only where there is no verifier (essay writing) or where an outside simulator checks the answer. Tree of Thoughts is argued to be prompt priming, not real search.
numbers: No new numbers in this passage.
limits: Opinion from a critical camp; contested by others who report gains from search.
agent_relevance: Do not count a model's critique of its own COA as testing. Count only outside checks.

source: Klein, Calderwood & Clinton-Cirocco (1986) Rapid decision making on the fire ground
finding: Fire commanders rarely compared options. They recognised a typical case and acted on the first workable option, checking it by mental simulation.
numbers: About 80% of 156 decisions were recognition-based with no option comparison (from memory, unchecked). Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature.
limits: Interview study with hindsight recall. Time pressure and expertise are the main moderators; no controlled test against multi-option planning.
agent_relevance: Doctrine's 'several COAs' conflicts with this. Several options may help novices, or when no pattern matches.

source: Klein, Wolf, Militello & Zsambok (1995) Skilled option generation in chess
finding: Strong chess players generated the best or near-best move first; the first move was usually the strongest they considered.
numbers: N and percentages not checked. Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature.
limits: Closed, structured domain; players unusually expert.
agent_relevance: Supports one good option then test, adding options only if the test fails.

source: Johnson & Raab (2003) Take the first: option generation and resulting choices
finding: In sport scenes, skilled players' first options were better than later ones; generating more options lowered choice quality.
numbers: Exact effect sizes unknown to me. Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature.
limits: Sport videos, not planning against a thinking opponent.
agent_relevance: After the first few, option quality falls. Cap the number of COAs.

source: Thunholm (2005) Planning under time pressure: prescriptive model of military tactical decision making
finding: Swedish Army studies of staffs under time pressure compared the full doctrinal planning process with a shortened one, and proposed a hasty-planning model.
numbers: Only the Crossref record was seen. No numbers recorded.
limits: Small staff samples; check the original.
agent_relevance: Time pressure is a moderator. A short mode may keep most of the gain.

source: Mitchell, Russo & Pennington (1989) Back to the future: temporal perspective in the explanation of events
finding: Imagining that an event has already happened (prospective hindsight) produced more and better reasons for it. This is the basis of the premortem.
numbers: About 30% more reasons identified (from memory, unchecked). Crossref record seen only.
limits: Small student samples; no trial of the premortem on plan quality (Klein 2007 builds on this).
agent_relevance: Cheap red-team step: assume the chosen COA failed and list why.

source: Schwenk (1990) Devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry: a meta-analysis
finding: Lab studies: both devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry gave better decisions than consensus groups; no clear difference between them.
numbers: Effect sizes unknown to me. Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature.
limits: Mostly student groups and case tasks; criticised for assigned advocates and expert-judged quality.
agent_relevance: Supports a forced-critic role even without a real enemy expert.

source: Cheikes, Brown, Lehner & Adelman (2004) Confirmation bias in complex analyses (MITRE)
finding: Intelligence-analysis experiment: structured method ACH did not remove confirmation bias overall; it helped mainly those less biased to start.
numbers: Details unchecked. Not opened this session; stated from memory of the literature.
limits: One case; narrow domain.
agent_relevance: A matrix or checklist is not a cure; test whether a COA scorecard changes outcomes.
